newsitem.title: USA: Alaska ballot measure targets airborne wolf hunts.
newsitem.headline: Alaska ballot measure targets airborne wolf hunts.

text.p: The perennial Alaska battle over wolves will be fought in voting booths this Election Day.

Wolf defenders, tired of state policy that allows hunters to track predators by airplane and shoot them after landing, gathered enough petition signatures to put a proposed ban on same-day aerial hunting on the Nov. 5 ballot.

"We feel that it is the single-most important vote in this decade as to how we in Alaska are going to manage our fish and wildlife," said Doug Pope, a co-chairman of the Wolf Management Reform Coalition, the group campaigning for the proposition.
Supporters of the measure say same-day aerial hunting is unethical and irresponsible.
Opponents of the measure lament what they say is a modern trend toward wolf admiration, replacing the belief that the animal competes with hunters for caribou and moose meat.

"Our way of life is under attack. Alaska is a frontier state. I grew up on the frontier when there was hardly anybody here," said Ed Grasser, an official with the Alaska Outdoor Council, a hunting organisation opposing the measure.

"Well that's changed and we've got a whole bunch of new people here. And those new people don't seem to want to respect the old-time values that people like I have that grew up here," Grasser said at a public hearing on Wednesday.
The last major eruption of the wolf controversy came four years ago when Gov. Wally Hickel promoted a state programme to thin out wild wolf packs by aerial shooting.
"You can't just let nature run wild," Hickel, a Republican, said in 1992, defending his plan to benefit sport hunters.
When Democratic Gov. Tony Knowles took office in late 1994, one of his first acts was to suspend the controversial wolf-control programme.
He asked for the National Academy of Sciences to review Alaska's predator management programmes, both for biological and economic soundness. The panel's report is expected in August.

But before Knowles' election the state Game Board enacted a regulation allowing anyone with a $15 trapping license to shoot an unlimited number of wolves, lynx, wolverines or other furbearers after landing an aircraft.
"This to me is not hunting," Jeanine Hurr, a Denali National Park tour bus driver, said of the practice. "This to me is a systematic extinction of a species."
Those favouring the ballot measure appear to have the big political guns, including Alaska celebrities as board members of the Wolf Management Reform Coalition.

One is former Gov. Jay Hammond -- the bearded, beret-wearing, poetry-writing, bush pilot and commercial fisherman who is probably the state's most beloved political figure. Another is former Lt. Gov. Lowell Thomas Jr., a famous bush pilot who served in Hammond's administration.
As of early October the coalition had amassed $93,078 in contributions. They came from Alaskans, environmental organisations and individuals spread from Vermont to Hawaii.
In contrast the Alaska Outdoor Council had raised only $7,010 to fight the ballot proposition by early October.
Only about 12 percent of Alaskans hold hunting licenses, according to the state Department of Fish and Game.
Anchorage pollster Dave Dittman said he believes the ballot proposition will pass because modern Alaskans object to the idea of "shotgunning from a Super Cub."
